title: Accessibility Rules!
text:
Title II

Refers to Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA)
Scope of Title II includes public entities such as:

Schools
Colleges
State and local governments
Healthcare providers

Don’t have to receive funding to fall under the scope of Title II

title: Accessibility Rules!
text:
Title II
Serves two main purposes:

Prohibits the discrimination of a disabled individual by previously described public entities
Requires all individuals be able to benefit from and access their services


Disabled does NOT always mean a disability someone was born with! Could also refer to an injury that happened to someone (permanent or not).

title: Accessibility Rules!
text:
Title II Examples

Elevators/ramps to access all areas of a building
Online government forms that anybody could access
Allowing service animals

“Accessible” = anyone can access

Accessible is easy to think about when it comes to something like a building. Not as easy to conceptualize when it comes to documents or online materials.

title: Accessibility Rules!
text:
Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG)

Department of Justice (DOJ) published a new rule under Title II in April 2024 regarding online accessibility regulations
Web content and other digital material must meet WCAG Version 2.1, Level AA standards

Levels range from A to AAA
AAA is highest level of accessibility

WCAG are developed by World Wide Web Consortium (W3C)

title: Accessibility Rules!
text:
WCAG Overview
Each guideline falls into one of four categories of the POUR acronym:

Perceivable
Operable
Understandable
Robust

The POUR acronym is commonly used to recall guidelines. A link to the full list of guidelines is in the “Resources” section of this presentation.

title: Accessibility Rules!
text:
Perceivable
“Information and user interface components must be presentable to users in ways they can perceive.”

Alternative (alt) text
Closed captioning/audio transcript
Color contrast/schemes
Text size and spacing
Display orientation

title: Accessibility Rules!
text:
Operable
“User interface components and navigation must be operable.”

Keyboard navigation
Keyboard focus is visible
Ability to adjust timed content
Content is in readable order (focus order)

title: Accessibility Rules!
text:
Understandable
“Information and the operation of the user interface must be understandable.”

No unusual language (slang) is used
Abbreviations are explained
Webpage navigation is consistent and predictable
Input fields provide assistance and error assistance

title: Accessibility Rules!
text:
Robust
“Content must be robust enough that it can be interpreted by a wide variety of user agents, including assistive technologies.”

Elements of a page or document are correctly tagged, labeled, and nested
Status messages can be presented to assistive technologies without receiving focus


Most HTML or XML based is considered to have met this criteria.

title: Chapter P
text: What do you think of when you hear the word “statistics”?

title: Chapter P
text:
Anecdotal Evidence
“I will never start jogging because my friend’s dad jogged his whole life, but he died at age 46 from a heart attack.”  “Don’t get your child vaccinated. I had my child vaccinated and now he is autistic.”  “My friend tried a new diet and lost weight so quickly- that diet must work really well.”

title: Chapter P
text: Statistics allow us to estimate something about a broad population.

title: Chapter P
text:
Helper vs. Hinderer


 
Link to Helper vs Hinderer Video

In a study reported in a November 2007 issue of Nature, researchers investigated whether infants take into account an individual’s actions towards others in evaluating that individual as appealing or aversive, perhaps laying the foundation for social interaction (Hamlin, Wynn, and Bloom, 2007).
The video describes the study that was done to test this theory, using “helper” and “hinderer” toys.

title: Chapter P
text:
The Six-Step Method Overview

Ask a research question
Design a study and collect data
Explore the data
Draw inferences beyond the data
Formulate conclusions
Look back and ahead

title: Chapter P
text:
1. Ask a research question

What do you want to know or investigate?
It does not have to be super specific

Helper vs. Hinderer example:

Do babies show a preference for the helper toy or the hinderer toy after being shown a puppet show?

We’re REALLY investigating nature vs. nurture

title: Chapter P
section: 2. Design a study and collect data
text:
2. Design a study and collect data

How will you test for your question?
What kind of data should be collected?

Helper vs. Hinderer example:

Recruit babies
Show each baby the puppet show
Record which toy the baby chooses

title: Chapter P
text:
3. Explore the data

Visually: Create boxplots, histograms, other graphs/charts
Numerically: Compute a number

Helper vs. Hinderer example:

14 picked the helper, 2 picked the hinderer

Proportionally: 14/16 = 0.875

title: Chapter P
text:
4. Draw inferences beyond the data

What might our results imply?
Did our data result from chance alone?
Is there an underlying cause?

Helper vs. Hinderer example:

Is 14/16 large enough to conclude babies prefer the helper toy?
Did 14 choose the helper by chance?

Perhaps the puppet show had an influence.

title: Chapter P
text:
5. Formulate conclusions

Strong evidence = form a conclusion
Weak evidence = data was inconclusive
Can often generalize to a population

Helper vs. Hinderer example

Conclusion: Babies preferred the helper toy over the hinderer toy, when shown the puppet show.
Can we say this about all babies?

title: Chapter P
text:
6. Look back and ahead

What was good about the experiment?
What could be improved?
Future research?

Helper vs. Hinderer example:

Recruit more babies

title: Chapter P
text:
Four Pillars of Statistical Evidence

Significance: How strong is the evidence of an effect?
Estimation: What is the size of the effect?
Generalization: How broadly do conclusions apply?
Causation: Can we say what caused the observed difference?


Typically, the pillars apply during step 4 or 5 of the six-step process.

title: Section 1.4
text:
Hypothesis Testing Review

Hypotheses refine our research question
We have two hypotheses:

Null hypothesis = what is believed to be true
Alternative hypothesis = what we think is actually true

Notation:

\(H_{0}: \pi = hypothesized\: value\)
\(H_{A}: \pi >,<,≠ hypothesized\: value\)

title: Section 1.4
text:
P-value Review

Tests for evidence in favor of \(H_{A}\)
Gives probability of observed statistic (\(\hat{p}\)) under null hypothesis
Calculating the p-value:

Count the # of simulated statistics as or more extreme than \(\hat{p}\) in the direction of the null hypothesis
Divide by total number of simulated statistics

title: Section 1.4
text:
P-value Review

If p-value > .05, fail to reject the null
If p-value ≤ .05, reject the null, accept alternative
Interpret based on context

title: Section 1.4
text:
Standardized Statistic Review

Another way to test for strength of evidence in favor of \(H_{A}\)
Obtain the standard deviation (SD)
Calculate the standardized statistic (\(z\)) by:

\[z=\frac{Observed\: Statistic - Hypothesized\: Value}{Standard\: Deviation\: under\: the\: null}\]

title: Section 1.4
text:
Standardized Statistic Review

If \(z\) > 2 or \(z\) < -2, reject the null, accept alternative
Interpret based on context of the problem

title: Section 1.4
text:
We always want stronger evidence against the null
Smaller p-value = stronger evidence
Larger standardized statistic absolute value = stronger evidence

title: Section 1.4
text:
Factors that impact evidence strength

Distance between observed statistic & null value
Sample size (n)
One-sided or two-sided hypothesis test

title: Section 1.4
text:
1. Distance from the null value
Recall: The null value is what we expect based on chance alone

Is the center of the null distribution

title: Section 1.4
text:
1. Distance from the null value
Consider \(\hat{p}\).

Further from null value = less likely null value is plausible

P-value is smaller, standardized statistic absolute value is larger

Closer to the null value = more likely null value is plausible

P-value is larger, standardized statistic absolute value is smaller

title: Section 1.4
text: 1. Distance from the null value

title: Section 1.4
text:
2. Sample Size

Increasing sample size increases strength of evidence
Decreasing sample size decreases strength of evidence

title: Section 1.4
text: 2. Sample Size

title: Section 1.4
text:
3. One-sided or two-sided hypothesis test
One-sided test:

Researchers think observed data will be greater than/less than the null model

Two-sided test:

Researchers don’t know; just looking for a difference

title: Section 1.4
text:
3. One-sided or two-sided hypothesis test
One-sided or two-sided refers to the form \(H_{A}\) takes.

One-sided test takes the form:

\[H_{A}: \pi > OR < hypothesized\: value\]

Two-sided test takes the form:

\[H_{A}: \pi ≠ hypothesized\: value\]

title: Section 1.2
text:
Hypothesis Testing

Allows us to summarize and refine our research question.
Step 1 in the six-step process

title: Section 1.2
text:
Hypothesis Testing (cont.)

Two hypotheses
Null hypothesis (\(H_{0}\)):

The chance explanation.
What we assume is true

Alternative hypothesis (\(H_{A}\)):

What researchers think could be true.
There’s an underlying cause.


We can either write our hypotheses in words or symbols.

title: Section 1.2
text:
Hypothesis Testing (cont.)
In words:

Null Hypothesis: The long run proportion of (variable of interest) is equal to (hypothesized proportion).
Alt. Hypothesis: The long run proportion of (variable of interest) is (less than/greater than/not equal to hypothesized proportion).

title: Section 1.2
text:
Hypothesis Testing (cont.)
In symbols:

\(H_{0}\): \(\pi\) = (hypothesized proportion)
\(H_{A}\): \(\pi\) >,<,≠ (hypothesized proportion)

Note that our hypothesized proportion will not be the same as our observed statistic!

title: Section 1.2
text:
Helper vs. Hinderer: Hypothesis Testing
In words:

Null: The long run proportion of times a baby chooses the helper toy is equal to 0.5
Alternative: The long run proportion of times a baby chooses the helper toy is greater than 0.5



In symbols:

\(H_{0}\): \(\pi\) = 0.5
\(H_{A}\): \(\pi\) = 0.5


  Where does 0.5 (1/2) come from?

title: Section 1.2
text:
Rock, Paper, Scissors: Hypothesis Testing
Research Question: Is scissors thrown less often than rock or paper?

We’re interested in \(\pi\), the long run proportion of times someone picks scissors.
What might a good hypothesized value for \(\pi\) be?

title: Section 1.2
text:
Rock, Paper, Scissors: Hypothesis Testing
In words:

Null: The long run proportion of times a person throws scissors is equal to 1/3.
Alt: The long run proportion of times a person throws scissors is less than 1/3.



In symbols:

\(H_{0}: \pi = \frac{1}{3}\)
\(H_{A}: \pi < \frac{1}{3}\)


  Why are we using “<”?

section: Rock, Paper, Scissors: Three S Strategy
text:
Rock, Paper, Scissors: Three S Strategy

Strength of Evidence: How likely is your observed statistic against the simulation?

“Eyeballing it” is not reliable
Need a concrete method
Enter p-value…

title: Section 1.2
text:
P-value



Reliable way to measure strength of evidence
P-value: The probability of obtaining a simulated value of the statistic as or more extreme than the observed statistic when the null hypothesis is true.

title: Section 1.2
text:
P-value



Always between 1 and 0
Represents the proportion of simulated statistics as or more extreme than the observed statistic, in the direction of the alternative hypothesis
Smaller p-value = stronger evidence against the null

(Aka, in favor of our alternative!)

title: Section 1.2
text:
P-value Cutoffs








P –value > .10

Not much evidence against the null hypothesis


.05 < p-value ≤ .10

Moderate evidence against the null hypothesis


.01 < p-value ≤ .05

Strong evidence against the null hypothesis


.01 ≤ p-value

Very strong evidence against the null hypothesis

title: Section 1.2
section: Hypothesis Testing and the Null Distribution
text:
Hypothesis Testing and the Null Distribution
The Applet generates a null distribution

Null Distribution: Simulated trials under the chance model
Will center at hypothesized value

Link to One Proportion Applet

title: Section 1.2
section: Hypothesis Testing and the Null Distribution (cont.)
text:
Hypothesis Testing and the Null Distribution (cont.)


Rock, paper, scissors simulation example

Observed statistic (\(\hat{p}\)): 2/20
P-value = 0.02

Based on this p-value, we would reject the null hypothesis.

title: Section 1.2
text:
Drawing Conclusions from the P-value


Remember, we start out assuming our null hypothesis is true.

title: Section 1.2
text:
Drawing Conclusions from the P-value
If p-value ≤ .05:

Reject the null hypothesis
Observed statistic likely didn’t occur by chance

title: Section 1.2
text:
Drawing Conclusions from the P-value
If p-value > .05:

Fail to reject the null hypothesis
Observed statistic could have happened by chance

title: Section 1.2
text:
Putting it into words
If we reject our null hypothesis (p-value ≤ 0.05):

We have enough evidence to conclude (insert alternative hypothesis here).

title: Section 1.2
text:
Putting it into words
If we fail to reject our null hypothesis (p-value > 0.05):

We do not have enough evidence to conclude (insert alternative hypothesis here).

text:

title: Section 2.2
text:
Type I Error

We reject the null hypothesis, but it is actually true
“False alarm”
In the Buzz and Doris example:

We conclude that Buzz is communicating with Doris, but he is guessing

title: Section 2.2
text:
Type II Error

We fail to reject the null hypothesis, but it is actually false
“Missed opportunity”
In the Buzz and Doris example:

We conclude that Buzz is just guessing, but really, he is communicating with Doris

If a Type II Error is made:

We have missed a potentially important result

Theory Based Approach (Quantitative Variable)
Validity conditions:

The variable of interest should have a symmetric distribution, or,

title: Section 2.3
text:
Theory Based Approach (Quantitative Variable)

With numerical data, we can find \(s\) (sample standard deviation)
This changes our standardized statistic calculation

\[SE=\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\]

title: Section 2.3
text:
Theory Based Approach (Quantitative Variable)

With numerical data, we use “\(t\)” instead of “\(z\)” to describe our standardized statistic

\[Standardized\: Statistic\:= t=\frac{\bar{x}-\mu}{SE}=\frac{\bar{x}-\mu}{\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}}\]

title: Section 2.3
text:
Drawing Conclusions

Same as categorical data

“Outside the twos” = reject the null
Otherwise fail to reject (FTR)

title: Section 2.3
text:
Drawing Conclusions
Conclusions take the same form:

Restate the alt. hypothesis

“We have enough evidence to conclude that the long-run average is (greater than/less than/not equal to) _____.”
“We do not have enough evidence to conclude that the long-run average is (greater than/less than/not equal to) _____.”

title: Section 2.3
text:
CEO Example




Sample size: n=30
Can we use the theory based approach? Yes
Observed statistic: \(\bar{x}\)=10.2
Sample standard deviation: \(s\)=2.091








Scenario




You are interested in whether the number of emails the CEO of Apple receives each day is more than 8. Suppose you observe 30 days and find that the average number of emails is 10.2, with a sample S.D. of 2.091. The distribution is not strongly skewed.

title: Section 2.3
text:
CEO Example
Standard error:
\[SE=\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}=\frac{2.091}{\sqrt{30}}=0.38\]
Standardized statistic:
\[ t=\frac{\bar{x}-\mu}{SE}=\frac{10.2-8}{0.38}=5.78\]

title: Section 2.3
text:
CEO Example Conclusion
“We have enough evidence to conclude that the long run average number of emails the CEO receives in a day is greater than 8.”

title: Section 3.1
text:
Significance Level
P-value cutoff for rejecting/failing to reject the null

Denoted by \(\alpha\)
More “mathematical” reason we reject \(H_{0}\) if p-value is less than 0.05
Significance level + confidence level = 100%

title: Section 3.1
text:
Common Significance Levels: \(\alpha\) = 0.10

90% confidence level
Reject when p-value < 0.10
Reject null more often
Narrower confidence interval
More Type I errors, less Type II errors

title: Section 3.1
text:

95% confidence level
Reject when p-value < 0.10
Standard Practice

title: Section 3.1
text:

99% confidence level
Reject when p-value < 0.01
Reject null less often
Wider confidence interval
Less Type I errors, more Type II errors

title: Section 1.1
text:
Doris and Buzz
In 1964, two dolphins (Doris and Buzz) were trained to push one of two buttons in a pool in reaction to a light. If the light flashed, the dolphins pushed the button on the left to get a fish. If the light was constant, the dolphins needed to push the button on the right.
Once they learned this behavior, the dolphins were separated by a wall (only Doris could see the light; only Buzz could push the buttons). To get a fish, Doris would need to communicate with Buzz.
The researcher, randomly deciding to make the light shine constant or flash, tested the dolphins’ ability to communicate.
Out of 16 attempts, the dolphins pushed the correct button 15 times.

title: Section 1.1
text:
We use the “Three S” Strategy



1: Statistic
Compute a statistic from the sample data.

2: Simulate
Develop a chance model. Repeatedly simulate values of the statistic under this model.

3: Strength of Evidence
Decide if the observed statistic was likely based on the simulation.

title: Section 1.1
text:
1. Statistic
Compute a statistic from the observed data.

Called our observed statistic.

Doris and Buzz example:


The proportion of times Buzz pushed the correct button

15/16 = observed statistic

title: Section 1.1
text:
2. Simulate

Develop a “chance model” (aka, a null model)
Chance model = what we would expect to happen at random, assuming there is no underlying cause
Under the chance models, repeatedly simulate values for our observed statistic.
This develops a sampling distribution (aka, a null distribution)


How might we simulate Doris and Buzz’s experiment?

title: Section 1.1
text:
3. Strength of Evidence
Based on our simulated values, is our observed statistic likely?

If the observed statistic seems likely:


The chance (null) model was possible.
Our results could’ve happened by random chance alone


If the observed statistic seems unlikely:


Our chance (null) model likely wasn’t possible
There’s probably some underlying cause

section: Wait, what is it we’re trying to do?
text:
Wait, what is it we’re trying to do?
Goal: Test if we have evidence in favor of our research question.

To do this, we design a study
We collect and test our data

title: Section 1.3
text:
Hypothesis Testing Review

Hypotheses refine our research question
Give us a precise idea of what we want to test
We have two hypotheses:

Null hypothesis
Alternative hypothesis

title: Section 1.3
text:
Hypothesis Testing Review

Null hypothesis (\(H_{0}\)):

The chance explanation.
What we assume is true

Alternative hypothesis (\(H_{A}\)):

What researchers think could be true.
There’s an underlying cause.


We can either write our hypotheses in words or symbols.

title: Section 1.3
text:
P-value Review
Once we have our hypotheses, we can test them.

P-value gives the probability of \(\hat{p}\) occurring if we assume \(H_{0}\) is true


We go by the following rules:

If p-value > .05, fail to reject the null
If p-value ≤ .05, reject the null, accept alternative

Then we interpret our results based on the context of the problem.

title: Section 1.3
text:
Standardized Statistic Method

A second method for determining strength of evidence
Standardizes \(\hat{p}\) to a standard normal distribution
Standard normal distribution = Normal distribution with mean of 0 and standard deviation of 1

title: Section 1.3
text:
Standard Deviation
Measure of how spread out data points are from the center.

title: Section 1.3
text:
Standardized Statistic
How many standard deviations an observed statistic is from the mean of the null distribution; denoted by \(z\)

title: Section 1.3
text:
Calculating the Standardized Statistic
\[z=\frac{Observed\: Statistic - Hypothesized\: Value}{Standard\: Deviation\: under\: the\: null}\]

title: Section 1.3
text:
Calculating the Standardized Statistic
Can alternatively be written as:
\[z=\frac{Observed\: Statistic - Mean\: under\: the\: null}{Standard\: Deviation\: under\: the\: null}\]
Note: “Hypothesized value” and “mean under the null” refer to the same value

title: Section 1.3
text:
Standardized Statistic

\(z\) can be negative OR positive
\(z\) represents the number of standard deviations the observed statistic is from the mean of the null distribution
The higher the absolute value of \(z\) is, the more evidence we have in favor of \(H_{A}\)
Absolute value =

Positive values stay the same
Negative values become their positive counterpart

title: Section 1.3
text:
Standard Deviation (S.D.) Formula
\[\sigma = \sqrt{\frac{\sum_{i=0}^n (x_{i}-\bar{x})^2}{n}}\]
Thankfully, you won’t need to know this formula for this course, but some of you might find it nice to know how this magical number is calculated.

Instead, we can get our s.d. using the Applet. (Phew!)

title: Section 1.3
text:
Obtaining Standard Deviation
Check “summary statistics” box to obtain the S.D.

Note: Your s.d. won’t be the same every time. How come?

text:
Heart Transplant Example

Observed statistic (\(\hat{p}\)) = 0.8
Hypothesized value (\(\pi\)) = 0.15
Standard Deviation under the null = 0.116 (from previous slide)

\[z=\frac{0.8 - 0.15}{0.116}=5.60\]
Cool, but what does this tell us?

title: Section 1.3
section: Evidence Based on the Standardized Statistic
text:
Evidence Based on the Standardized Statistic

Like the p-value, we have criteria for rejecting or failing to reject the null based on the standardized statistic (s.s.)
Reject \(H_{0}\) when the s.s. is below -2 or above 2
“Outside the twos”

title: Section 1.5
text:
Simulation
So far, we’ve used a simulation-based approach to gather strength of evidence.

Effective
Relatively easy

But…

Can be tedious
Not always practical in real life
Enter: Theory!

title: Section 1.5
text:
The Theory-Based Approach

Used when computers weren’t a thing
Allows prediction of the null distribution shape (aka, pattern)
Gives us p-values and standardized statistics
Should get the same or similar results as simulation

title: Section 1.5
text:
The Null Distribution (in depth!)

Sometimes, data follows a known distribution
Commonly, we assume data follows the normal distribution
The normal distribution is one of many known patterns that data can follow
In this class, we always assume the null distribution is normally distributed

title: Section 1.5
text:
The Null Distribution (in depth!)
Since we know the null distribution is normally distributed, we know the following:

Bell shaped
Centered at \(\pi\)
Can predict standard deviation

Without the Applet!

title: Section 1.5
text: Example Null Distribution

title: Section 1.5
text:
Why does sample size matter?
If sample size is too small:

Theory-based approach will not be accurate
Curve might not be bell-shaped

Theory-based “rule of thumb”:

Need at least 10 successes and 10 failures

title: Section 1.5
text:
To illustrate…















Both are centered at 0.50
Left graph n = 30
Right graph n = 300

title: Section 1.5
text:
Central Limit Theorem

“Backbone” of statistics

Definition:

If the sample size (n) is large enough, the distribution of the sample proportions will be bell-shaped (approximately normal), centered at the long run probability (\(\pi\)), with a standard deviation:

\[standard\: deviation\: of\: the\: null=\sqrt{\frac{\pi(1-\pi)}{n}}\]

title: Section 1.5
text:
Using Theory for Standardized Values
Replace S.D. with theory-based calculation
\[z=\frac{Observed\: Statistic - Hypothesized\: Value}{Standard\: Deviation\: under\: the\: null}\]
\[=\frac{\hat{p}-\pi}{\sqrt{\frac{\pi(1-\pi)}{n}}}\]

title: Section 1.5
text:
Halloween Treats


Let’s identify the following:

Sample & size:
Variable of interest:
Parameter & symbol:
Observed statistic & symbol:
Hypotheses (in symbols):

Do we meet the criteria for the theory-based approach?







Scenario:




Researchers investigated whether children might be as tempted by toys as by candy for Halloween treats. Test households offered two plates to children: one with candy and one with a small toy. They observed the selections of 283 children that night and found that 148 of the kids chose candy.

title: Section 1.5
text:
Halloween Treats

Sample & size: n = 283 kids
Variable of interest: Chose candy or not
Parameter & symbol: \(\pi\) = long run proportion of kids that chose candy
Observed statistic & symbol: \(\hat{p} = \frac{148}{283}\)
Hypotheses (in symbols):

\(H_{0}\): \(\pi\) = 0.5
\(H_{A}\): \(\pi\) ≠ 0.5


Do we meet the criteria for the theory-based approach? Yes! More than 10 failures & successes.

title: Section 1.5
text:
Halloween Treats
Standard deviation using theory:
\[standard\: deviation\: of\: the\: null=\sqrt{\frac{\pi(1-\pi)}{n}}\]
\[=\sqrt{\frac{0.5(1-0.5)}{283}}=0.0297\]

title: Section 1.5
text:
Halloween Treats
Then, we use the calculated standard deviation to obtain the standardized statistic:
\[standardized\: statistic\: =\frac{0.523-0.5}{0.0297}=0.774\]

title: Section 1.5
text:
Halloween Treats
Now we find the standardized statistic with the simulation approach:
\[standardized\: statistic\: =\frac{0.523-0.5}{0.02}=0.793\]
Notice, we get nearly the same number!

title: Section 1.5
text:
Halloween Treats Conclusion
Since our standardized statistic using either approach is not outside the twos, we conclude the following:  “We do not have enough evidence to conclude that the long-run proportion of kids who choose candy differs from 0.5.”
